title: When Guidance Becomes a Guard:Early Interception of Unsafe Inputs in Text-to-Image Generation

paper.title: When Guidance Becomes a Guard: Early Interception of Unsafe Inputs in Text-to-Image Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Text-to-image diffusion models can produce unsafe content,
while output filtering intervenes only after synthesis.
We investigate whether native generation signals enable
early detection of unsafe and adversarial inputs.
We find that classifier-free guidance exposes strong safety
signals in conditional responses, accessible through
compact statistics and linear readouts.
Based on this finding, we propose Conditional Semantic
Trajectory Interception (CSTI), which aggregates activation
contrasts between conditional and unconditional responses
at early checkpoints for calibrated risk detection.
CSTI fits concept-specific detectors using canonical concept
and safe examples, without attack samples, intermediate
image decoding, or generator modification.
Across five generators, four adversarial attack collections,
and two general NSFW datasets, CSTI achieves the strongest
overall performance among six baselines at a matched 5% FPR.
Early interception reduces generation latency by over
60% on intercepted paths.
These results demonstrate the effectiveness of native
conditional responses for early safety interception.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image models can generate compelling visual content from natural language prompts [ 23 ] , but can also be exploited to produce unsafe images. Crafted prompts may bypass safeguards and induce explicit nudity, violence, or other harmful content [ 31 , 43 ] . Final image moderation can block such outputs only after the full generation cost is incurred. This motivates early interception before synthesis is complete while allowing benign requests to proceed normally, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Figure 1 : From late checking to early interception. (a) Crafted prompts can induce unsafe generations. (b) Post-generation safety checks incur the full generation cost. (c) In this example, CSTI reads early CFG activations at steps 5, 10, and 15, intercepting risky inputs while allowing accepted requests to continue unchanged. Intermediate images are shown only for illustration. Recent work has shown that safety can be assessed during generation. IGD classifies predicted noise [ 41 ] , Wukong detects from intermediate features while reusing cross-attention parameters [ 17 ] , and FlowGuard projects intermediate latents into an approximate image space for visual detection [ 42 ] . These methods demonstrate the feasibility of in-generation detection, but leave room to examine the safety information already present in the generator’s native conditional computation. Effective interception requires high sensitivity to unsafe and adversarial inputs while minimizing false rejections of benign requests, further motivating the study of early diffusion representations. This motivates a question. How early does a text-to-image generator become safety-readable, and how little machinery is needed to read that signal? We investigate this question through the native computation of classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 12 ] . CFG evaluates conditional and unconditional branches from the same latent state at each sampling update. We find that differences between their internal activations already contain strong safety information at early sampling stages. Compact channel statistics preserve much of this information, which can be effectively recovered using simple linear readouts. These observations suggest that the computation used to guide image formation also provides accessible safety signals before synthesis is complete. Based on this finding, we introduce Conditional Semantic Trajectory Interception ( CSTI ). CSTI summarizes conditional activation contrasts at a few early checkpoints into a compact representation and applies a lightweight linear risk readout. Under our 50-update protocol, CSTI observes updates 5, 10, and 15 and makes a single decision after update 15. Flagged generations terminate early, while accepted generations continue along the original sampling trajectory. CSTI requires no intermediate image decoding, external visual encoder, or modification of the generator. For each generator and risk concept, the detector is fitted using canonical concept examples and safe examples without attack samples. An independent safe set is used to calibrate the interception threshold, separating concept fitting from threshold selection. Neither process relies on the adversarial prompt collections used for evaluation. We evaluate CSTI on five generators: SD1.4 and SD1.5 [ 23 ] , SDXL [ 22 ] , SD3.5 Medium [ 6 , 28 ] , and Z-Image [ 47 , 30 ] , spanning U-Net and Transformer backbones. CSTI achieves the strongest overall performance among representative baselines on nudity and violence collections at a matched 5% FPR. Layer, checkpoint, and classifier analyses confirm that simple linear readouts can exploit early safety signals. CSTI reduces generation latency by over 60% on intercepted paths across all five generators. Our contributions are threefold: • We reveal that native conditional responses of text-to-image generators contain strong safety signals at early sampling stages, which can be effectively extracted using compact statistics and simple linear readouts. • We propose CSTI, a lightweight interception framework that requires no attack examples for detector fitting, no intermediate image decoding, and no modification of the generator or accepted sampling process. • We systematically evaluate CSTI, demonstrating the effectiveness of early safety signals and the computational efficiency of interception.

sections.heading: Safety defenses and adversarial prompts.
sections.text: Safety mechanisms for text-to-image generation operate at different stages. Before sampling, text classifiers such as the NSFW Text Classifier [ 21 ] and Detoxify [ 11 ] can screen potentially unsafe requests. Latent Guard [ 18 ] detects harmful concepts in learned representations of text encoder embeddings, while GuardT2I [ 44 ] uses a language model to convert text guidance embeddings into natural language for adversarial prompt detection. Such screening can reject risky requests before synthesis, but does not observe how the generative state develops during sampling. Other defenses change how images are generated. ESD [ 7 ] removes target concepts by updating model weights, whereas SLD [ 24 ] and CRG [ 5 ] suppress unsafe concepts through inference-time guidance. Adversarial methods such as Ring-A-Bell [ 31 ] and MMA-Diffusion [ 43 ] demonstrate that crafted prompts can still elicit unsafe outputs despite existing safeguards. Together, these approaches motivate examining whether risk can be assessed during generation without changing accepted sampling. sections.heading: Safety detection during generation.
sections.text: Recent methods inspect intermediate model states to identify unsafe content before the final image is available. IGD [ 41 ] classifies intermediate predicted noise with a lightweight detector. Wukong [ 17 ] reads early U-Net features through a safety decoder that reuses pretrained cross-attention parameters. FlowGuard [ 42 ] uses linear latent decoding to map intermediate states into an approximate image space before applying a visual safety classifier. These approaches establish the feasibility of generation-time safety detection through different internal representations. Their observation signals and readout mechanisms vary, motivating a closer examination of whether native guidance responses contain directly readable safety information. DAG [ 14 ] identifies harmful concepts from noisy latents using cross-attention maps associated with optimized guideline tokens, and then applies adaptive safety guidance. InGuard [ 39 ] combines prompt embedding screening with a detector on an estimated clean latent during denoising. CSTI examines a different source of safety information. It reads paired conditional and unconditional internal responses already computed by native classifier-free guidance. Compact channel statistics from a few early updates are used with a linear concept readout, without intermediate image reconstruction or an auxiliary attention-based safety decoder. Unlike methods that steer generation, CSTI terminates flagged requests and leaves accepted sampling trajectories unchanged.

sections.heading: Generative representations and safety calibration.
sections.text: Research on diffusion features shows that internal generative representations can support discriminative tasks beyond image synthesis. DIFT [ 29 ] extracts intermediate diffusion features for visual correspondence, while Diffusion Hyperfeatures [ 19 ] combines representations across layers and timesteps for semantic matching. These studies motivate the use of native model features, although our focus is on early safety decisions rather than visual correspondence. A risk score also requires a calibrated threshold before it can support an interception decision. Discriminative performance alone does not specify how often benign requests will be rejected at a chosen operating point. Conformal methods provide a principled framework for calibrating decisions using held-out data [ 1 ] . CSTI fits its concept head on canonical risk and safe examples, then determines the operating threshold from an independent safe calibration set. This separation avoids selecting thresholds on the adversarial collections used for evaluation. Figure 2 : Overview of CSTI. (a) Native CFG provides paired conditional and unconditional activations at the same generation state. Their difference forms a conditional contrast. (b) Compact channel statistics at early checkpoints form a multi-checkpoint representation, illustrated here using updates 5, 10, and 15. (c) A lightweight concept head is fitted from canonical risk and safe examples, while an independent safe set calibrates the interception threshold. In this example, CSTI decides once at update 15.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We introduce Conditional Semantic Trajectory Interception ( CSTI ) to detect unsafe inputs from native internal responses before image synthesis is complete. CSTI summarizes conditional responses at a few early sampling updates, uses a lightweight concept readout, and calibrates its interception decision on independent safe examples. The generator remains frozen throughout fitting and deployment. Figure 2 illustrates the framework. Consider a text-to-image generator G G , a prompt p p , a random seed r r , and a defender-specified risk concept c c . Let z ( 0 ) z^{(0)} be the initial generation state and z ( t ) z^{(t)} the state after sampling update t t , with T T updates in total. At update t t , the generator evaluates its model using the preceding state z ( t − 1 ) z^{(t-1)} . CSTI makes one interception decision after an early update h < T h<T . We use T = 50 T=50 and h = 15 h=15 throughout the main evaluation.

sections.heading: 3.2 Concept Adaptation without Attack Examples
sections.text: CSTI fits a risk readout for each generator and defender-specified concept using canonical concept examples and safe examples. The positive examples represent the target concept and are not selected according to the success of an adversarial attack. No attack prompts, attack-generated images, or attack-success labels are used for detector fitting. Given the early representation x x , we standardize its features and apply a whitened PCA projection with 128 components, v ⁡ ( x ) = PCA 128 white ⁡ ( Std ⁡ ( x ) ) . v(x)=\operatorname{PCA}_{128}^{\mathrm{white}}\bigl(\operatorname{Std}(x)\bigr). (5) A linear head then produces a concept-specific risk score, s c ​ ( x ) = w c 𝖳 ​ v ​ ( x ) + b c . s_{c}(x)=w_{c}^{\mathsf{T}}v(x)+b_{c}. (6) We use class-balanced logistic regression and take its linear decision value as the risk score, with larger values indicating greater risk. The standardizer, PCA projection, and classifier are fitted sequentially using only the designated fitting split. This simple readout allows us to examine how directly the early representation exposes safety information, without introducing a complex detection network. Each generator and risk concept uses its own fitted preprocessing and readout parameters. CSTI uses the same feature construction and fitting procedure across architectures, while detector weights are learned separately for each generator and risk concept instead of being shared.

sections.heading: 3.3 Safe-Calibrated Early Interception
sections.text: A risk score must be converted into an interception decision. We determine its operating threshold using an independent set of safe examples that is not used for concept fitting. After fitting the readout, let s 1 , … , s n cal s_{1},\ldots,s_{n_{\mathrm{cal}}} denote the risk scores of these calibration examples. For a test risk score s s , we compute its upper-tail rank relative to the safe calibration scores, p safe ​ ( s ) = 1 + ∑ i = 1 n cal 𝟏 [ s i ≥ s ] n cal + 1 . p_{\mathrm{safe}}(s)=\frac{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{cal}}}\mathbf{1}[s_{i}\geq s]}{n_{\mathrm{cal}}+1}. (7) A small value indicates that the test score is unusually high relative to the safe reference distribution. Given an operating level α \alpha , the interception decision is f c ( p , r ; G ) = [ p safe ( s c ( x ) ) ≤ α ] . f_{c}(p,r;G)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[p_{\mathrm{safe}}\bigl(s_{c}(x)\bigr)\leq\alpha\right]. (8) The fitted readout and calibration rule remain fixed across attack collections for each generator and concept. The quantity p safe p_{\mathrm{safe}} is a ranking score, not the probability that the input is benign When calibration and test safe examples are exchangeable, this rank rule bounds the marginal false-positive rate at the chosen level α \alpha [ 1 ] . Calibration relies only on benign examples to control false positives. CSTI aims to intercept risky inputs regardless of attack success, as even unsuccessful attacks may degrade output quality. During sampling, CSTI records summaries at updates 5, 10, and 15 and makes a single decision after update h = 15 h=15 . Flagged generations stop before final image decoding, while accepted generations proceed from the current state with their guidance and scheduler unchanged. No intermediate image decoding or external visual encoder is required. Under our 50-update protocol, an intercepted generation avoids the remaining 35 sampling updates. The corresponding runtime reduction is measured separately in Section 4 .

sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: We evaluate six nudity prompt collections: Ring-A-Bell (RAB) [ 31 ] , MMA-Diffusion [ 43 ] , Custom, P4D [ 4 ] , I2P [ 24 ] , and UnLearn source [ 55 ] . For violence, we use RAB and I2P. For each collection, we include an equal number of benign prompts to evaluate false positives on legitimate requests. For over-refusal, we use OVERT-mini [ 3 ] .

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: We evaluate five unmodified text-to-image generators: SD1.4, SD1.5, SDXL, SD3.5 Medium, and full Z-Image. All use 50 sampling updates. SD1.4/1.5 and SDXL use DDIM [ 25 ] with CFG 7.5 at 512 2 512^{2} and 1024 2 1024^{2} resolution, respectively. SD3.5 Medium and Z-Image use FlowMatch Euler [ 16 ] at 1024 2 1024^{2} , with CFG 7.5 and 5, respectively. Experiments run on an NVIDIA RTX 4090.

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: CSTI observes updates { 5 , 10 , 15 } \{5,10,15\} and makes a single decision at update 15. We extract features from the U-Net middle block, SD3.5 Transformer block 11, or Z-Image layer 14, respectively. Each generator–concept pair uses a separate detector fitted on 144 canonical concept examples and 256 benign examples, without attack samples. Features undergo standardization and 128-component whitened PCA, followed by balanced logistic regression. Independent benign sets are used for safety calibration (200 prompts, α = 0.075 \alpha=0.075 ) and evaluation (300 prompts).

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: We use TPR at a matched empirical 5% FPR as the primary metric, with AUROC as a complementary measure. TPR measures the proportion of unsafe inputs correctly detected. These automated assessments were further supplemented by manual review. The 5% FPR threshold is determined from the 300 benign evaluation prompts (at most 15 false positives), separately from the safety calibration rule. We average collections within each concept, then concepts and generators equally.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against three prompt-level detectors: NSFW Text Classifier [ 21 ] , Latent Guard [ 18 ] , and GuardT2I [ 44 ] ; and three generation-time detectors: IGD [ 41 ] , Wukong [ 17 ] , and DAG [ 14 ] (detection component only). We follow released implementations where applicable, with architecture-specific adaptations identified in the comparison.

sections.heading: 4.2 Early Interception Effectiveness
sections.text: Table 2 compares CSTI with six representative baselines at a matched 5 % 5\% FPR. CSTI achieves the highest TPR in 37 of 40 evaluation settings, with macro TPRs ranging from 92.39 % 92.39\% on SD3.5 Medium to 95.75 % 95.75\% on Z-Image. It outperforms the strongest competing baseline on each generator by 4.06 to 15.99 percentage points. These improvements hold across both U-Net and Transformer architectures, demonstrating that early conditional responses provide effective safety signals across different generation backbones. Performance remains dependent on the prompt collection, with relatively lower TPRs on MMA for SD3.5 Medium ( 78.35 % 78.35\% ) and I2P violence for SDXL ( 84.27 % 84.27\% ). sections.heading: 4.3 Characterizing Early Safety Readability
sections.text: We investigate where safety information is accessible, how early it can be detected, and how complex a readout is required. Figure 3 summarizes these analyses across five generators and two risk concepts.

sections.heading: Layer selection.
sections.text: Figure 3 (a) shows that safety information is accessible across multiple network layers, with intermediate layers generally providing stronger readability. On SDXL, nudity TPR increases from 73.57 % 73.57\% at the earliest examined layer to 97.62 % 97.62\% at the middle block. Similarly, violence TPR on Z-Image rises from 42.41 % 42.41\% at layer 0 to 95.50 % 95.50\% at layer 14. Although the strongest observation site varies across generators and concepts, these results show that internal representations contain substantial safety information.

sections.heading: Sampling stages.
sections.text: Figure 3 (b) shows that safety information is already strongly readable at update 5, achieving 88.4 % 88.4\% TPR for nudity and 85.2 % 85.2\% for violence at a matched 5 % 5\% FPR. Combining updates 5, 10, and 15 increases the overall macro TPR from 92.2 % 92.2\% at update 15 alone to 94.5 % 94.5\% . Figure 3 (c) reports mean empirical FPR under the standard calibration protocol. Each variant uses its own fitted classifier and calibrated threshold, without independently adjusting its empirical FPR to 5 % 5\% . The joint representation achieves a mean empirical FPR of 4.2 % 4.2\% , compared with 15.9 % 15.9\% , 13.5 % 13.5\% , and 10.4 % 10.4\% for updates 5, 10, and 15, respectively. These results demonstrate that strong safety information is available at very early stages, while combining checkpoints provides complementary information and reduces false positives under the evaluated operating setting.

sections.heading: Readout complexity.
sections.text: Figure 3 (d) compares linear and nonlinear classifiers on the same representation. Logistic regression achieves 96.5 % 96.5\% and 92.5 % 92.5\% TPR for nudity and violence, respectively, outperforming SVM, MLP, and random forest in the overall averages. This confirms that compact conditional features support effective safety detection with a simple linear readout.

sections.heading: 4.4 Over-Refusal Evaluation
sections.text: The matched FPR evaluation on standard benign prompts does not fully characterize false interceptions when safe requests resemble protected concepts. Legitimate requests should proceed without unnecessary rejection. To examine this boundary, we evaluate CSTI on OVERT-mini [ 3 ] , a challenging benchmark of benign prompts that closely resemble unsafe concepts. We select SD1.4 and SD3.5 to cover both U-Net and Transformer architectures. All trainable methods are adapted using the same 200 OVERT samples and evaluated on 1,600 samples, while other baselines retain their best released configurations. Table 4 reports the resulting FPR. CSTI achieves the lowest FPR of 5.27% on SD1.4, outperforming all six baselines. On SD3.5, CSTI reaches 8.25% FPR, ranking second and trailing DAG by only 0.14 percentage points. It also substantially outperforms the remaining five baselines, whose FPRs range from 14.20% to 38.43%. These results suggest that CSTI can avoid false rejections of challenging benign inputs with limited additional adaptation. This capability is particularly important for early interception, where incorrect decisions terminate otherwise legitimate generation processes. Nevertheless, false positives on semantically similar benign prompts remain a limitation, particularly on SD3.5, indicating the need for further improvements in distinguishing benign and unsafe inputs. sections.heading: 4.5 Computational Efficiency
sections.text: We evaluate the computational efficiency of CSTI across five generators under the 50-update sampling protocol. Table 5 shows that early termination at update 15 reduces execution latency by 61.41 % 61.41\% to 71.72 % 71.72\% across U-Net and Transformer architectures. Early termination also reduces peak GPU memory on SD1.4, SD1.5, and SDXL, while memory usage remains unchanged on SD3.5 Medium and Z-Image.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We investigated early safety signals in text-to-image diffusion models and found that native conditional responses enable effective detection of unsafe and adversarial inputs through compact statistics and simple linear readouts. Building on this finding, we introduced CSTI for calibrated early interception without attack samples, intermediate image decoding, or modification of accepted sampling. Experiments across five generators spanning U-Net and Transformer architectures demonstrate strong overall detection performance against representative baselines. Further analyses show that safety signals are accessible at early sampling stages and across multiple layers, while simple linear readouts remain effective. These findings demonstrate that native guidance computation provides an effective and efficient foundation for early safety interception.

sections.heading: Adversarial robustness and AI security.
sections.text: The security of deep learning systems has been extensively investigated across diverse adversarial settings. Existing research has explored adversarial perturbations and robustness [ 8 , 20 , 2 , 13 ] , as well as transferable attacks against visual and multimodal representations [ 27 , 26 , 37 ] . Related studies have also investigated adversarial manipulation of training data and learned representations, including unlearnable examples [ 33 , 36 ] . Beyond inference-time attacks, training-time threats such as data poisoning and model poisoning [ 52 , 15 ] , as well as backdoor attacks [ 10 , 56 , 50 ] , can compromise learned representations and induce unintended model behaviors. Corresponding detection mechanisms have also been investigated across different learning architectures and tasks [ 45 , 51 ] . These efforts highlight the broader importance of identifying adversarially induced behavior and developing reliable safeguards for increasingly capable AI systems.

sections.heading: Safety of foundation and generative models.
sections.text: As AI systems integrate language, vision, and decision-making capabilities, safety concerns have expanded beyond conventional discriminative prediction. Recent research has examined jailbreak attacks against large language models [ 57 , 53 ] , adversarial prompting and prompt injection in multimodal and agentic systems [ 9 , 49 , 32 ] , and adversarial behavioral manipulation of embodied agents [ 54 , 34 , 38 ] . Related security challenges also arise in visual generative models, where adversarial manipulation can affect image editing [ 48 ] , visual synthesis [ 35 ] , and the generation of unsafe or misleading content [ 40 , 46 ] . While these settings differ in their threat models and attack objectives, they underscore the need for safety mechanisms that extend beyond conventional input screening. In particular, generative models progressively construct their outputs through multiple computational stages, raising the question of whether emerging risks can be identified before synthesis is complete.

sections.heading: Safety defenses for text-to-image generation.
sections.text: Safety mechanisms for text-to-image generation operate at different stages of the generation pipeline. Before sampling, text classifiers such as the NSFW Text Classifier [ 21 ] and Detoxify [ 11 ] can screen potentially unsafe requests. Latent Guard [ 18 ] detects harmful concepts in text encoder representations, while GuardT2I [ 44 ] examines textual interpretations of guidance embeddings for adversarial prompt detection. Such screening can reject risky requests before synthesis, but does not observe how the generative state evolves during sampling. Other defenses directly modify the generation process. ESD [ 7 ] removes target concepts by updating model weights, whereas SLD [ 24 ] and CRG [ 5 ] suppress unsafe concepts through inference-time guidance. Nevertheless, adversarial prompting approaches such as Ring-A-Bell [ 31 ] and MMA-Diffusion [ 43 ] demonstrate that unsafe content can still be elicited despite existing safeguards. These limitations motivate safety assessment during generation, without modifying accepted sampling trajectories.

sections.heading: Intermediate representations and early safety detection.
sections.text: Recent studies investigate whether intermediate diffusion states can reveal safety-relevant information before the final image is available. IGD [ 41 ] classifies intermediate predicted noise, while Wukong [ 17 ] detects unsafe content from early U-Net features using an auxiliary safety decoder. FlowGuard [ 42 ] projects intermediate latents into an approximate image space for visual safety assessment. DAG [ 14 ] exploits cross-attention signals for harmful concept identification and adaptive guidance, whereas InGuard [ 39 ] combines prompt screening with detection on estimated clean latents. These approaches demonstrate the feasibility of assessing generation risk from intermediate computations, although their observation signals and intervention mechanisms differ. More broadly, diffusion representations have been shown to capture semantic information useful for discriminative tasks beyond image generation. DIFT [ 29 ] and Diffusion Hyperfeatures [ 19 ] demonstrate the utility of intermediate features across sampling stages and network layers. Such findings motivate examining the safety information encoded within the generator’s native computations. Moreover, reliable interception requires not only a discriminative risk score but also a calibrated decision threshold, for which held-out calibration provides a principled foundation [ 1 ] . In contrast to approaches that require intermediate image reconstruction, auxiliary safety decoders, or modification of the generation process, CSTI examines the paired conditional and unconditional activations already computed by classifier-free guidance. By aggregating compact channel statistics across early sampling checkpoints, CSTI extracts safety-relevant signals using a lightweight linear readout. An independent safe calibration set determines the interception threshold, while flagged generations terminate early and accepted trajectories remain unchanged. This design exploits native conditional computation to support efficient safety assessment before image synthesis is complete.

We investigate whether native generation signals enable early detection of unsafe and adversarial inputs. We find that classifier-free guidance exposes strong safety signals in conditional responses, accessible through compact statistics and linear readouts. Based on this finding, we propose Conditional Semantic Trajectory Interception (CSTI), which aggregates activation contrasts between conditional and unconditional responses at early checkpoints for calibrated risk detection. CSTI fits concept-specific detectors using canonical concept and safe examples, without attack samples, intermediate image decoding, or generator modification. Across five generators, four adversarial attack collections, and two general NSFW datasets, CSTI achieves the strongest overall performance among six baselines at a matched 5% FPR. Early interception reduces generation latency by over 60% on intercepted paths. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of native conditional responses for early safety interception. 1 Introduction Text-to-image models can generate compelling visual content from natural language prompts [ 23 ] , but can also be exploited to produce unsafe images. Crafted prompts may bypass safeguards and induce explicit nudity, violence, or other harmful content [ 31 , 43 ] . Final image moderation can block such outputs only after the full generation cost is incurred. This motivates early interception before synthesis is complete while allowing benign requests to proceed normally, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Figure 1 : From late checking to early interception. (a) Crafted prompts can induce unsafe generations. (b) Post-generation safety checks incur the full generation cost. (c) In this example, CSTI reads early CFG activations at steps 5, 10, and 15, intercepting risky inputs while allowing accepted requests to continue unchanged. Intermediate images are shown only for illustration. Recent work has shown that safety can be assessed during generation. IGD classifies predicted noise [ 41 ] , Wukong detects from intermediate features while reusing cross-attention parameters [ 17 ] , and FlowGuard projects intermediate latents into an approximate image space for visual detection [ 42 ] . These methods demonstrate the feasibility of in-generation detection, but leave room to examine the safety information already present in the generator’s native conditional computation. Effective interception requires high sensitivity to unsafe and adversarial inputs while minimizing false rejections of benign requests, further motivating the study of early diffusion representations. This motivates a question. How early does a text-to-image generator become safety-readable, and how little machinery is needed to read that signal? We investigate this question through the native computation of classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 12 ] . CFG evaluates conditional and unconditional branches from the same latent state at each sampling update. We find that differences between their internal activations already contain strong safety information at early sampling stages. Compact channel statistics preserve much of this information, which can be effectively recovered using simple linear readouts. These observations suggest that the computation used to guide image formation also provides accessible safety signals before synthesis is complete. Based on this finding, we introduce Conditional Semantic Trajectory Interception ( CSTI ). CSTI summarizes conditional activation contrasts at a few early checkpoints into a compact representation and applies a lightweight linear risk readout. Under our 50-update protocol, CSTI observes updates 5, 10, and 15 and makes a single decision after update 15. Flagged generations terminate early, while accepted generations continue along the original sampling trajectory. CSTI requires no intermediate image decoding, external visual encoder, or modification of the generator. For each generator and risk concept, the detector is fitted using canonical concept examples and safe examples without attack samples. An independent safe set is used to calibrate the interception threshold, separating concept fitting from threshold selection. Neither process relies on the adversarial prompt collections used for evaluation. We evaluate CSTI on five generators: SD1.4 and SD1.5 [ 23 ] , SDXL [ 22 ] , SD3.5 Medium [ 6 , 28 ] , and Z-Image [ 47 , 30 ] , spanning U-Net and Transformer backbones. CSTI achieves the strongest overall performance among representative baselines on nudity and violence collections at a matched 5% FPR. Layer, checkpoint, and classifier analyses confirm that simple linear readouts can exploit early safety signals. CSTI reduces generation latency by over 60% on intercepted paths across all five generators. Our contributions are threefold: • We reveal that native conditional responses of text-to-image generators contain strong safety signals at early sampling stages, which can be effectively extracted using compact statistics and simple linear readouts. • We propose CSTI, a lightweight interception framework that requires no attack examples for detector fitting, no intermediate image decoding, and no modification of the generator or accepted sampling process. • We systematically evaluate CSTI, demonstrating the effectiveness of early safety signals and the computational efficiency of interception. 2 Related Work Safety defenses and adversarial prompts. Safety mechanisms for text-to-image generation operate at different stages. Before sampling, text classifiers such as the NSFW Text Classifier [ 21 ] and Detoxify [ 11 ] can screen potentially unsafe requests. Latent Guard [ 18 ] detects harmful concepts in learned representations of text encoder embeddings, while GuardT2I [ 44 ] uses a language model to convert text guidance embeddings into natural language for adversarial prompt detection. Such screening can reject risky requests before synthesis, but does not observe how the generative state develops during sampling. Other defenses change how images are generated. ESD [ 7 ] removes target concepts by updating model weights, whereas SLD [ 24 ] and CRG [ 5 ] suppress unsafe concepts through inference-time guidance. Adversarial methods such as Ring-A-Bell [ 31 ] and MMA-Diffusion [ 43 ] demonstrate that crafted prompts can still elicit unsafe outputs despite existing safeguards. Together, these approaches motivate examining whether risk can be assessed during generation without changing accepted sampling. Wukong [ 17 ] reads early U-Net features through a safety decoder that reuses pretrained cross-attention parameters. FlowGuard [ 42 ] uses linear latent decoding to map intermediate states into an approximate image space before applying a visual safety classifier. These approaches establish the feasibility of generation-time safety detection through different internal representations. Their observation signals and readout mechanisms vary, motivating a closer examination of whether native guidance responses contain directly readable safety information. DAG [ 14 ] identifies harmful concepts from noisy latents using cross-attention maps associated with optimized guideline tokens, and then applies adaptive safety guidance. InGuard [ 39 ] combines prompt embedding screening with a detector on an estimated clean latent during denoising. CSTI examines a different source of safety information. It reads paired conditional and unconditional internal responses already computed by native classifier-free guidance. Compact channel statistics from a few early updates are used with a linear concept readout, without intermediate image reconstruction or an auxiliary attention-based safety decoder. Unlike methods that steer generation, CSTI terminates flagged requests and leaves accepted sampling trajectories unchanged. Generative representations and safety calibration. Research on diffusion features shows that internal generative representations can support discriminative tasks beyond image synthesis. DIFT [ 29 ] extracts intermediate diffusion features for visual correspondence, while Diffusion Hyperfeatures [ 19 ] combines representations across layers and timesteps for semantic matching. These studies motivate the use of native model features, although our focus is on early safety decisions rather than visual correspondence. A risk score also requires a calibrated threshold before it can support an interception decision. Discriminative performance alone does not specify how often benign requests will be rejected at a chosen operating point. Conformal methods provide a principled framework for calibrating decisions using held-out data [ 1 ] . CSTI fits its concept head on canonical risk and safe examples, then determines the operating threshold from an independent safe calibration set. Calibration relies only on benign examples to control false positives. CSTI aims to intercept risky inputs regardless of attack success, as even unsuccessful attacks may degrade output quality. During sampling, CSTI records summaries at updates 5, 10, and 15 and makes a single decision after update h = 15 h=15 . Setup Datasets. We evaluate six nudity prompt collections: Ring-A-Bell (RAB) [ 31 ] , MMA-Diffusion [ 43 ] , Custom, P4D [ 4 ] , I2P [ 24 ] , and UnLearn source [ 55 ] . For violence, we use RAB and I2P. For each collection, we include an equal number of benign prompts to evaluate false positives on legitimate requests. For over-refusal, we use OVERT-mini [ 3 ] . Models. We evaluate five unmodified text-to-image generators: SD1.4, SD1.5, SDXL, SD3.5 Medium, and full Z-Image. All use 50 sampling updates. SD1.4/1.5 and SDXL use DDIM [ 25 ] with CFG 7.5 at 512 2 512^{2} and 1024 2 1024^{2} resolution, respectively. SD3.5 Medium and Z-Image use FlowMatch Euler [ 16 ] at 1024 2 1024^{2} , with CFG 7.5 and 5, respectively. Experiments run on an NVIDIA RTX 4090. Implementation. CSTI observes updates { 5 , 10 , 15 } \{5,10,15\} and makes a single decision at update 15. We extract features from the U-Net middle block, SD3.5 Transformer block 11, or Z-Image layer 14, respectively. Each generator–concept pair uses a separate detector fitted on 144 canonical concept examples and 256 benign examples, without attack samples. Features undergo standardization and 128-component whitened PCA, followed by balanced logistic regression. Independent benign sets are used for safety calibration (200 prompts, α = 0.075 \alpha=0.075 ) and evaluation (300 prompts). Metrics. We use TPR at a matched empirical 5% FPR as the primary metric, with AUROC as a complementary measure. TPR measures the proportion of unsafe inputs correctly detected. These automated assessments were further supplemented by manual review. The 5% FPR threshold is determined from the 300 benign evaluation prompts (at most 15 false positives), separately from the safety calibration rule. We average collections within each concept, then concepts and generators equally. Baselines. Building on this finding, we introduced CSTI for calibrated early interception without attack samples, intermediate image decoding, or modification of accepted sampling.
